Characteristic exponent (eλt)

Words: 29
Linear ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
A characteristic exponent is a value λ for which an exponential mode eλt solves the homogeneous constant-coefficient linear equation or system. Repeated exponents can give polynomial factors multiplying that exponential.

Fundamental system of solutions (y1​,…,yn​)

Words: 74
Linear ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
A fundamental system for a homogeneous linear ordinary differential equation of order n on an interval is a basis of its vector space of homogeneous solutions. Every solution has a unique expression ∑j=1n​cj​yj​ with constant coefficients. Under the usual continuity assumptions and a nonvanishing leading coefficient, a nonzero Wronskian at one point proves that n solutions form such a system: their initial-value vectors are independent and span all possible initial data, and the Picard-Lindelöf theorem supplies uniqueness. For a first-order vector system, the corresponding columns form a fundamental matrix.

Fourier response of a first-order linear differential equation (y​n​=g​n​/(a+in))

Words: 119
Linear ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
For y′+ay=g with real a>0 and 2π-periodic forcing, comparing Fourier coefficients gives (a+in)y​n​=g​n​. There is no vanishing denominator, including the constant mode. With real cosine and sine coefficients an​,bn​ for g and An​,Bn​ for y, the equivalent equations give
An​=a2+n2aan​−nbn​​,Bn​=a2+n2nan​+abn​​.
(1)
Whenever termwise differentiation is justified, these formulas construct a periodic particular solution. For a forcing series with coefficients O(n−2), the differentiated response coefficients are also summable, which supplies such a justification by uniform convergence. All other solutions add the homogeneous solution Ce−ax. Since this exponential cannot be periodic unless C=0, the periodic solution is unique. This is also a simple example of how a linear equation changes the amplitude and phase of each harmonic independently.

Words: 24
Linear ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
A linear second-order ordinary differential equation with periodic coefficient. For accelerator beam optics, s measures distance along the reference orbit and k(s) is the local transverse focusing strength.

Oscillatory-root criterion for a real second-order equation (a12​−4a0​a2​<0)

Words: 61
Linear ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
For real constants with a2​=0, a nonzero solution of the homogeneous linear differential equation a2​f′′+a1​f′+a0​f=0 has a sinusoidal factor exactly when the discriminant a12​−4a0​a2​ is negative. Indeed the characteristic polynomial has roots −a1​/(2a2​)±iω, where ω=4a0​a2​−a12​​/(2∣a2​∣), giving f=e−a1​t/(2a2​)(C1​cosωt+C2​sinωt). Real or repeated roots instead give real exponential functions, possibly multiplied by a linear polynomial. Oscillatory behaviour and decay are separate: decay requires a1​/a2​>0.

Exponential substitution removing a constant first derivative (y=eaxu:y′′−2ay′+(a2+b2)y=eax(u′′+b2u))

Words: 54
Linear ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
Differentiating y=eaxu twice proves the displayed identity. It converts an exponentially weighted forced equation into a simple harmonic oscillator equation. If b=0, the reduced homogeneous solutions are 1,x rather than cosbx,sinbx as an independent pair. If the forcing contains a term at frequency ∣b∣, resonance requires an additional polynomial factor in a particular solution.

Constant-coefficient differential equation (an​y(n)+⋯+a1​y′+a0​y=f(x))

Words: 37
Linear ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
A linear ordinary differential equation has constant coefficients when the multipliers aj​ of the unknown function and its derivatives do not depend on the independent variable. The forcing f may still vary. For the homogeneous equation f=0, its characteristic equation of a constant-coefficient differential equation determines exponential solutions.

Power substitution reducing a differential equation to constant coefficients (y=xnz)

Words: 61
Linear ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
On an interval where the substitution is real and x=0, a factor formed by exponentiation can remove inverse powers from the coefficients of a linear ordinary differential equation. For
y′′+(a+xb​)y′+(c+xd​+x2e​)y=0,
(2)
the substitution y=xnz gives
z′′+(a+x2n+b​)z′+(c+xan+d​+x2n(n−1)+bn+e​)z=0.
(3)
It becomes a constant-coefficient differential equation exactly when 2n+b=0, an+d=0 and n(n−1)+bn+e=0. Derive this by the product rule; checking only the coefficient of z′ is insufficient.

Exponential forcing response with zero initial data ((D−a)(D−b)y=ecx,y(0)=y′(0)=0)

Words: 79
Linear ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
For pairwise distinct rates a,b,c, the response is
y=(a−b)(a−c)eax​+(b−a)(b−c)ebx​+(c−a)(c−b)ecx​.
(4)
Set v=y′−by. Solving v′−av=ecx with v(0)=0 gives (ecx−eax)/(c−a); solving the remaining first-order equation by an integrating factor gives the formula. Equivalently this is the convolution of ecx with the zero-displacement unit-impulse response (eax−ebx)/(a−b) on the positive half-line. In the resonant case c=b=a, the finite limit is y=[eax−ebx−(a−b)xebx]/(a−b)2. The apparent singularity of the distinct-rate expression is removable, and the limit exhibits the polynomial factor of a resonant exponential particular solution.

Product-derivative reduction of a second-order differential equation (py′′+2p′y′+p′′y=(py)′′)

Words: 79
Linear ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
Recognizing the displayed product derivative reduces a homogeneous second-order equation to (py)′′=0. On any interval where p=0, its general solution is y=(A+Bx)/p. For p=1−x3, the equation becomes (1−x3)y′′−6x2y′−6xy=0. Data y(0)=1, y′(0)=0 give 1/(1−x3)=∑j≥0​x3j, with radius of convergence one. The poles occur at the three cube roots of unity. A solution singularity can disappear for a special numerator that cancels the corresponding factor, so an equation's singular point need not be a singularity of every solution.

Characteristic equation of a constant-coefficient differential equation (P(r)=0)

Words: 61
Linear ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
For the homogeneous linear ordinary differential equation ∑j=0n​aj​y(j)=0, substitute y=erx. Dividing by the nonzero exponential gives the polynomial equation P(r)=∑j​aj​rj=0. A simple root gives an exponential solution; a root of multiplicity m gives xkerx for 0≤k<m. Real equations admit real sine and cosine combinations of conjugate roots. These characteristic roots determine growth, decay and oscillation of the linearized modes.

Method of undetermined coefficients

Words: 188 Articles: 2
Linear ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
Choose a finite trial family of polynomial-exponential or trigonometric functions for a particular solution, substitute it into a constant-coefficient linear equation, and solve for its coefficients. If the forcing exponent is a characteristic root of multiplicity m, multiply the ordinary trial by tm to leave the homogeneous kernel. The method is efficient for forcing families preserved by differentiation.

Complex forcing method for a real differential equation

Words: 66
Method of undetermined coefficients OurBigBook.com
For a real linear differential operator L, one has L(Imu)=Im(Lu). A forcing term written as the imaginary part of a polynomial times eiωx can therefore be handled by solving one complex equation, then taking the imaginary part. For L=d2/dx2+a, substituting u=p(x)eiωx gives p′′+2iωp′+(a−ω2)p. If the forcing frequency is resonant, the polynomial ansatz must include the appropriate additional power of x.

Resonant exponential particular solution (yp​=xerx/P′(r))

Words: 64
Method of undetermined coefficients OurBigBook.com
For a constant-coefficient linear differential equation P(D)y=erx, where D denotes differentiation, a simple root P(r)=0 forces a resonant trial. Factor P(z)=(z−r)Q(z); since (D−r)(xerx)=erx, commuting the differential operators gives P(D)(xerx)=Q(r)erx=P′(r)erx. Thus the displayed expression is a particular solution. More generally, if the root has multiplicity m, the same factorization gives P(D)(xmerx)=P(m)(r)erx, so yp​=xmerx/P(m)(r). This is the extra polynomial factor required by resonance in a differential equation.

Weighted energy estimate for two coupled modes (N=c∣A∣2+a∣B∣2)

Words: 46
Linear ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
Suppose two complex amplitudes satisfy ∂t​∣A∣2≤2a∣A∣∣B∣−2d∣A∣2 and ∂t​∣B∣2≤2c∣A∣∣B∣−2d∣B∣2, with positive a,c and d≥0. Then N=c∣A∣2+a∣B∣2≥2ac​∣A∣∣B∣ gives N˙≤2(ac​−d)N. A positive weighted norm avoids treating two coupling rates of different size as a single arithmetic sum. This is useful for nonautonomous linear ordinary differential equations and the bounded-modulation alpha-Omega growth estimate.

Newton's law of cooling (y′=−k(y−Ta​))

Words: 364 Articles: 4
Linear ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
Newton's law of cooling models an object's temperature y using a positive constant rate k and ambient temperature Ta​. The displayed ordinary differential equation assumes one temperature represents the object, the environment remains at Ta​, and the proportional rate stays fixed over the modeled range. It also describes warming when y<Ta​. These are modeling assumptions: [ref] explain the proportional law through a tangent line approximation and caution about large temperature differences.
Dimensional analysis requires k to have units of inverse time. The product k(t−t0​) in the exponential function solution is therefore dimensionless. The equilibrium point y=Ta​ attracts both warmer and colder starting states: the excess temperature undergoes exponential decay. See initial value problem for computed cooling times, direction field for the family of trajectories, and separable differential equation for a derivation.

Impulse versus finite-duration cooling (θ′+aθ=−F(t))

Words: 91
Newton's law of cooling OurBigBook.com
For equal initial temperatures and the same Newton's law of cooling coefficient a>0, compare a unit Dirac delta function cooling impulse at time one with unit-rate cooling on the interval from one to two. The impulse produces a temperature jump of minus one. The finite-duration forcing gives a continuous temperature with change −(1−e−a(t−1))/a while it is active. Relative to the common unforced cooling curve, the impulse contributes −e−a(t−1). Consequently the temperatures cross at t=1+log(1+a)/a, strictly between one and two. After time two the impulse-cooled body is warmer: the later cooling receives less subsequent exponential attenuation.

Cumulative thermal destruction under exponential warming and cooling (D(T)=βmax​[T−e−αT(1−e−αT)/α])

Words: 66
Newton's law of cooling OurBigBook.com
In an ideal linear temperature-dependent destruction model with equal warming and cooling durations, normalized temperature is 1−e−αt during warming and (1−e−αT)e−α(t−T) during cooling. Integrating the destruction rate gives D(T), the logarithm of the surviving-count reduction factor. If the endpoint destruction rate and thermal relaxation constant stay fixed, changing the temperature gap alone leaves this integral unchanged. This is a property of the stipulated model.

Newton cooling with an instantaneous temperature jump

Words: 51
Newton's law of cooling OurBigBook.com
Under Newton's law of cooling with fixed ambient temperature T0​ and k>0, an instantaneous jump β at t∗​ sets T(t∗​+)=T(t∗​−)+β. The subsequent temperature is T0​+[T(t∗​−)+β−T0​]e−k(t−t∗​). Equivalently, for an initial temperature Ti​, the full solution is
T(t)=T0​+(Ti​−T0​)e−kt+βH(t−t∗​)e−k(t−t∗​).
(5)
This piecewise model has the distributional derivative equation T′+k(T−T0​)=βδ(t−t∗​), with the Dirac delta distribution representing the added temperature.

Heat transfer coefficient (λ)

Words: 44
Newton's law of cooling OurBigBook.com
A heat transfer coefficient relates heat flux through a boundary to a temperature difference: F=λΔT. Its dimensions are power per area per temperature. In a quasistatic ice layer, atmospheric boundary resistance 1/λA​ and conductive resistance h/k add in series, giving effective conductance (1/λA​+h/k)−1.

Homogeneous solution

Words: 49
Linear ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
A homogeneous solution solves the associated linear equation with zero forcing. The difference of any two solutions to the same forced linear equation is homogeneous.
A homogeneous solution satisfies the associated homogeneous linear differential equation, obtained by setting the forcing term to zero. Such solutions form the kernel of the differential operator.

Particular solution

Words: 26
Linear ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
A particular solution is any one solution of a forced linear differential equation. Every solution is the sum of that particular solution and an arbitrary homogeneous solution.

General solution

Words: 33
Linear ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
The general solution of a differential equation is a family containing every solution, usually parameterized by arbitrary constants or initial data. For a forced linear ordinary differential equation, it is the sum of one particular solution and the general homogeneous solution.

Dominant eigenmode in a forced linear system

Words: 33
Linear ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
After diagonalising a constant-coefficient system, each eigenmode satisfies a scalar forced equation. The large-time behaviour is determined by the largest exponential rate whose coefficient does not vanish, including rates introduced by the forcing.

Second-order linear differential equation

Words: 4k Articles: 66
Linear ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
A second-order linear equation has the form y′′+p(x)y′+q(x)y=f(x).

Point interaction in a second-order differential equation (Lα​y=y′′+αy(c)δc​)

Words: 317 Articles: 2
Second-order linear differential equation OurBigBook.com
A point interaction concentrates a coefficient of a linear differential equation at a single interior point. On an interval 0<x<ℓ, with 0<c<ℓ, consider Lα​y=y′′+αy(c)δc​. The domain consists of continuous functions that are twice differentiable away from c, with the required one-sided derivatives. Multiplication of the Dirac delta by y means the unambiguous point value y(c)δc​. It does not mean an undefined product of a delta with an arbitrary discontinuous function.
The equation is interpreted using distributional derivatives. Smooth forcing gives an ordinary equation on each side, with transmission conditions for a delta coefficient at the interaction. A delta potential in the one-dimensional Schrödinger equation is a physical example after choosing the corresponding sign and constants.

Dirichlet resonance for a point interaction (α∗​=ℓ/(c(ℓ−c)))

Words: 137
Point interaction in a second-order differential equation OurBigBook.com
The boundary value problem y′′+αy(c)δc​=f on (0,ℓ) with Dirichlet boundary conditions has a unique solution for every continuous forcing and prescribed endpoint values exactly when α=α∗​:=ℓ/(c(ℓ−c)). The left-normalized homogeneous solution is
uα​(x)=x−αc(x−c)+​,uα​(ℓ)=ℓ−αc(ℓ−c),
(6)
where (t)+​=max(t,0). Continuity at c and the transmission conditions for a delta coefficient give this formula. The final boundary condition fixes the initial slope unless the displayed endpoint value is zero. This is a one-dimensional kernel obstruction, analogous to the Fredholm alternative.
At resonance the normalized null function is
ϕ(x)={x/c,(ℓ−x)/(ℓ−c),​0≤x≤c,c≤x≤ℓ.​
(7)
For y(0)=a and y(ℓ)=b, the compatibility condition is
∫0ℓ​ϕ(x)f(x)dx=ca​+ℓ−cb​.
(8)
Indeed, integrate ϕLα​y−yLα​ϕ on both sides of c. The internal terms cancel by the matching derivative jumps, leaving [ϕy′−ϕ′y]0ℓ​. This equals the right-hand side. The initial-slope construction also proves sufficiency: when compatible there is a one-parameter family y0​+tϕ; otherwise no solution exists.

Transmission conditions for a delta coefficient ([y]c​=0,[y′]c​+αy(c)=J)

Words: 77
Point interaction in a second-order differential equation OurBigBook.com
For a point interaction in a second-order differential equation, the equation y′′+αy(c)δc​=f+Jδc​, with nonsingular continuous f, requires
[y]c​=0,[y′]c​+αy(c)=J.
(9)
The distributional second derivative across a jump explains both conditions: there is no derivative-of-delta source to balance a value jump, and the coefficients of the delta source must agree. In particular, without a point source, [y′]c​=−αy(c). With a unit point source at the same location, the condition is [y′]c​=1−αy(c); one must combine the two contributions rather than impose two incompatible jump conditions.

Laguerre differential equation (xy′′+(1−x)y′+νy=0)

Words: 102 Articles: 1
Second-order linear differential equation OurBigBook.com
This equation has a regular singular point at zero and an irregular singular point at infinity. For a nonnegative integer ν=n, the solution analytic at zero with value one is the Laguerre polynomial Ln​. Its weighted self-adjoint form is (xe−xy′)′+νe−xy=0, connecting it to the Laguerre differential operator on polynomials.

Frobenius series for the Laguerre differential equation (ak+1​=(k+1)2k−ν​ak​)

Words: 62
Laguerre differential equation OurBigBook.com
A Frobenius solution y=∑k≥0​ak​xk+σ has the repeated indicial root σ=0. Equating coefficients gives the displayed recurrence relation. The resulting analytic solution is an entire function: its consecutive term ratio has magnitude asymptotic to ∣x∣/k. For ν=n≥0 an integer, the recurrence terminates and Ln​(x)=∑k=0n​(−1)k(kn​)xk/k!. The second local solution is independent and has a logarithmic term at zero; repeated indicial roots do not supply two independent analytic series.

Quadratic-variable reduction of a singular oscillator (xy′′−y′+4x3y=0,u=x2)

Words: 53
Second-order linear differential equation OurBigBook.com
The chain rule with y(x)=Y(x2) gives xy′′−y′=4x3Y′′ and transforms the equation, away from zero, into Y′′+Y=0. Thus its solution space is spanned by cos(x2) and sin(x2). Both extend smoothly through the regular singular point at zero. Their even power series allow the independent data y(0) and y′′(0) to select the two solutions; every smooth solution has y′(0)=0.

Repeated-root constant-coefficient differential equation ((D−r)2y=f)

Words: 45
Second-order linear differential equation OurBigBook.com
The homogeneous equation has linearly independent solutions erx and xerx, with nonzero Wronskian e2rx. Setting y=erxu converts the forced equation to u′′=e−rxf. For resonant forcing f=erx, the particular response is x2erx/2. This substitution explains the extra powers of x required by repeated-root resonance.

Singular point of a second-order linear ODE

Words: 54
Second-order linear differential equation OurBigBook.com
For a normalized second-order equation, a point is singular when its coefficient functions are not both analytic there. If multiplying them by the first and second powers of distance to the point makes them analytic, it is a regular singular point. This classification concerns the equation; some individual solutions may nevertheless extend analytically through the point.

Reciprocal-coordinate reduction of a beam-type equation (u=t[Acos(λ/t)+Bsin(λ/t)])

Words: 34
Second-order linear differential equation OurBigBook.com
For t>0, the change of variables τ=1/t and u(t)=v(τ)/τ converts t4u′′+λ2u=0 into v′′+λ2v=0. The chain rule gives u′=v−τv′ and u′′=τ3v′′. Thus u=t[Acos(λ/t)+Bsin(λ/t)]. The prefactor cancels the derivative term introduced by inverting the independent variable.

Liouville transformation of a second-order equation (U=x˙−1/2u(x(t)))

Words: 44
Second-order linear differential equation OurBigBook.com
A smooth invertible change of variables in uxx​−f(x)u=0 introduces a first derivative in time. Rescaling by x˙−1/2 removes it. Choosing x˙=f−1/2 locally for f>0 produces the constant leading coefficient used in the WKB approximation; negative f requires a complex branch or the corresponding oscillatory real formulation.

Power substitution for an oscillatory second-order equation

Words: 41
Second-order linear differential equation OurBigBook.com
For γ=0 and x>0, the change of variables u=xγ converts
x2−2γy′′+(1−γ)x1−2γy′+γ2y=0
(10)
into Yuu​+Y=0, where y(x)=Y(u). The chain rule cancels the first-derivative terms. Thus cos(xγ) and sin(xγ) form a pair of linearly independent solutions, with Wronskian γxγ−1. This is a variable-speed reparametrization of the harmonic oscillator equation.

Mathieu equation (u′′+(a−2qcos2t)u=0)

Words: 95 Articles: 1
Second-order linear differential equation OurBigBook.com
The Mathieu equation is the displayed linear differential equation with periodic coefficients. Floquet theory describes its bounded and exponentially growing solutions, while its periodic Mathieu characteristic values mark the edges of parametric resonance gaps. The forcing normalization matters: replacing t by t/2 rescales both the constant and periodic coefficients.

Mathieu characteristic value (an​(q), bn​(q))

Words: 56
Mathieu equation OurBigBook.com
The Mathieu characteristic values are the parameter values a for which the Mathieu equation has the even periodic mode traditionally denoted cen​, or the odd periodic mode sen​. They are eigenvalues of −d2/dt2+2qcos2t with the corresponding periodic or antiperiodic boundary conditions. Their small-q expansions can be derived by projecting onto a Fourier series and perturbing the resulting tridiagonal matrix.

Airy ordinary differential equation (f′′(Z)−Zf(Z)=0)

Wronskian (W(f,g)=fg′−f′g)

Words: 724 Articles: 2
Second-order linear differential equation OurBigBook.com
For two differentiable functions f,g on an interval I, their Wronskian is the function
W(f,g)(x)=det(f(x)f′(x)​g(x)g′(x)​)=f(x)g′(x)−f′(x)g(x).
(21)
The order matters: exchanging f and g reverses the sign. For n sufficiently differentiable functions, the Wronskian is the determinant det(fj(i−1)​(x))i,j=1n​.[ref]
The Wronskian measures whether the vectors (f(x),f′(x)) and (g(x),g′(x)) supply independent value-and-derivative data at that point. For real-valued functions, its absolute value is the area of the parallelogram they span. If a constant linear combination af+bg is zero throughout I, then af′+bg′=0 too. A nonzero Wronskian at even one point makes this pair of linear equations invertible and forces a=b=0. Thus a nonzero Wronskian somewhere always proves linear independence of the functions on I.
For an explicit example, the exponential functions
y1​(x)=e−x,y2​(x)=e2x
(22)
solve the same homogeneous linear differential equation y′′−y′−2y=0 on the whole real line: substitution gives 1+1−2=0 and 4−2−2=0, respectively. Their Wronskian is
W(y1​,y2​)=e−x(2e2x)−(−e−x)e2x=3ex>0.
(23)
For the initial value problem y(0)=2, y′(0)=−1, the linear combination y=c1​y1​+c2​y2​ requires c1​+c2​=2 and −c1​+2c2​=−1. Hence c1​=5/3, c2​=1/3, and y=35​e−x+31​e2x. The nonzero Wronskian makes the two initial conditions independently adjustable.
The stronger converse requires a common equation. Suppose y1​,y2​ solve y′′+p(x)y′+q(x)y=0 with continuous functions p,q on one interval I. Then the functions are linearly independent if and only if their Wronskian is nonzero at one point, equivalently at every point. If W(x0​)=0, choose constants a,b, not both zero, making z=ay1​+by2​ satisfy z(x0​)=z′(x0​)=0. The superposition principle makes z a solution of a differential equation for the same equation, and the uniqueness theorem for ordinary differential equations forces z to be identically zero. This proves linear dependence.[ref]
For arbitrary differentiable functions, an identically zero Wronskian need not imply linear dependence. Consider, on I=(−2,2),
f(x)=x4,g(x)=x∣x∣3={−x4,x4,​x<0,x≥0.​
(24)
Both functions have three continuous derivatives. On each side of zero, g is a constant multiple of f, so W(f,g)=0; at zero their values and first derivatives are all zero, so the Wronskian is zero there too. Nevertheless af+bg=0 evaluated at x=−1 gives a−b=0, while evaluation at x=1 gives a+b=0. Hence a=b=0: these functions are linearly independent on the whole interval. There is no single constant multiplier valid on both sides of the common zero.
These functions cannot both solve any equation y′′+py′+qy=0 with continuous functions p,q throughout (−2,2): even f alone would contradict uniqueness because f(0)=f′(0)=0 but f is not identically zero. They do solve the singular equation x2y′′−3xy′=0, whose leading coefficient vanishes at zero. Dividing by x2 gives p=−3/x only away from zero; Abel's identity cannot be applied across that point. The example pinpoints why checking the equation and its interval is essential before using a zero Wronskian to infer linear dependence.

Vanishing Wronskian does not imply linear dependence

Words: 94
Wronskian OurBigBook.com
Two differentiable functions can be linearly independent on a connected interval while their Wronskian vanishes everywhere. For example, let f(x)=(max{−x,0})2 and g(x)=(max{x,0})2. Both have a continuous first derivative, and their values and first derivatives vanish at zero. On either side of zero one of the functions is identically zero, so fg′−f′g=0 everywhere. Evaluating a constant linear combination Af+Bg=0 at −1 and 1 forces A=B=0.
The obstruction is that the two halves supply independent information without simultaneous nonzero value-and-derivative data at any point. For solutions of a common regular second-order linear differential equation, the uniqueness theorem for ordinary differential equations removes this possibility; Abel's identity gives the zero-or-nowhere-zero alternative for their Wronskian.

on an interval I where p,q are continuous functions. For any x0​∈I, Abel's identity gives

The exponential function is positive for real p, so a real Wronskian either vanishes everywhere or has a fixed nonzero sign throughout I. In the preceding example, p=−1 and W(0)=3 give W(x)=3ex immediately. If p=0, every Wronskian of two solutions of a differential equation for that same equation is constant, regardless of q. Thus Abel's identity can certify linear independence and find the denominator used in variation of parameters without explicit formulas for both solutions of a differential equation.

Legendre polynomial evaluation representer (qn​(t)=∑j=0n​pj​(0)​pj​(t))
Words: 92
Legendre polynomial OurBigBook.com
For orthonormal Legendre polynomials on [−1,1], the polynomial qn​ represents evaluation at zero on polynomials of degree at most n: ⟨r,qn​⟩=r(0). This follows by expanding r in the orthonormal basis, or from the Riesz representation theorem. With M=⌊n/2⌋ and cm​=(m2m​)/4m, orthonormality gives
∥qn​∥22​=21​∑m=0M​(4m+1)cm2​=2(2M+1)2cM2​​.
(35)
The last identity telescopes using cm​/cm−1​=(2m−1)/(2m). The norms are unbounded: cm​≥1/(2m+1) makes the sum dominate a divergent harmonic series. Thus the evaluation identities hold eventually for every fixed polynomial but cannot extend to convergence for every L2 vector, by the Uniform boundedness principle. Point evaluation is also not defined on L2 equivalence classes.

For normalized Legendre polynomials pn​=(2n+1)/2​Pn​, parity makes the sign function orthogonal to every even index. Integrating the Legendre differential equation gives ∫01​Pn​=Pn′​(0)/(n(n+1)). The differentiated generating function z(1+z2)−3/2 gives the derivatives at zero and hence the displayed odd coefficients. The Parseval identity and squared norm two then evaluate ∑m≥0​((2m)!)2(4m+3)/[24m(m!(m+1)!)2]=4.
Rodrigues formula for Legendre polynomials (Pl​(x)=2ll!1​dxldl​(x2−1)l)
Words: 75
Legendre polynomial OurBigBook.com
This instance of Rodrigues' formula constructs the Legendre polynomial for every nonnegative integer l. Put v=(x2−1)l; then (x2−1)v′=2lxv. Differentiating l+1 times by the Leibniz rule gives (x2−1)y′′+2xy′−l(l+1)y=0 for y=v(l), which is the Legendre differential equation after reversing signs. The leading term of the normalized derivative is (2l)!xl/[2l(l!)2], proving its polynomial degree is exactly l. At x=1, the product (x+1)l(x−1)l contributes only the term with all l derivatives on the second factor, giving v(l)(1)=2ll!. Thus the normalization is Pl​(1)=1.

The endpoint term vanishes because of (1−x2)2, giving the displayed weighted orthogonality. The zero polynomial R0​ is not a nonzero eigenfunction.

Boundedness at zero removes x−n−1, and the value at t=1 makes an​=xn. Orthogonality then gives ∫−11​G2dt=∑n​kn​x2n. The integral is x−1log((1+x)/(1−x)), so kn​=2/(2n+1). Uniform analyticity on compact subdiscs ∣x∣<1 justifies the generating expansion and termwise calculations.

Finite-pulse response of a first-order linear equation (y(t)=A[λeλ(t−a)−1​H(t−a)−λeλ(t−b)−1​H(t−b)])

Words: 102
First-order linear differential equation OurBigBook.com
Let 0<a<b and y′−λy=A[H(t−a)−H(t−b)], with zero initial data. For λ=0, the Laplace transform time-shift rule gives the displayed response, since the transform of the input is A(e−as−e−bs)/s and the equation supplies the factor (s−λ)−1. Equivalently, integrate the impulse response eλtH(t) over the active pulse. Before a the solution is zero; during the pulse it is A(eλ(t−a)−1)/λ; after b it is Aeλt(e−λa−e−λb)/λ. The solution is continuous at both switching times. At λ=0 take the limit, giving linear growth during the pulse and the constant A(b−a) afterward. Positive λ gives growing memory, while negative λ gives decay after forcing stops.

Causal response of a first-order relaxation equation (G(t)=α−1e−t/αH(t))

Words: 79
First-order linear differential equation OurBigBook.com
For α>0, the retarded impulse response of αy′+y=f is the displayed function, with H the Heaviside step function. The corresponding convolution y(t)=α−1∫−∞t​e−(t−s)/αf(s)ds is the unique solution tending to zero in the remote past whenever the integral exists and has that limit. For example, bounded forcing that tends to zero as t→−∞ satisfies these conditions. A general forcing need not: f≡1 admits no such solution. A unit-duration pulse with α=1 gives y=0 before zero, y=1−e−t between zero and one, and y=(1−e−1)e−(t−1) thereafter.

Integrating factor (μ(t)=exp(∫t0​t​a(s)ds))

Words: 996 Articles: 6
Linear ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
An integrating factor is a nonzero multiplier that makes a differential equation directly integrable. For a first-order linear differential equation, it gathers the unknown function and its derivative into one product rule expression. Suppose a and b are continuous functions on an interval containing t0​, and consider the initial value problem
y′+a(t)y=b(t),y(t0​)=y0​.
(42)
Define A(t)=∫t0​t​a(s)ds and μ(t)=eA(t). The exact solution of a differential equation throughout that interval is
y(t)=e−A(t)[y0​+∫t0​t​eA(s)b(s)ds].
(43)
The definite integral fixes μ(t0​)=1, so the initial condition appears without an extra constant to determine. If the equation originally has a coefficient multiplying y′, first divide by that coefficient on an interval where it is nonzero; a zero of that coefficient needs separate attention. See OpenStax's first-order linear equations chapter for this normalization and the integrating factor procedure.
For a concrete balance, solve y′+2y=3 with y(0)=0. Here μ=e2t, so multiplying the entire ordinary differential equation gives (e2ty)′=3e2t. Accumulating from zero to t gives
e2ty(t)=∫0t​3e2sds=23​(e2t−1),y(t)=23​(1−e−2t).
(44)
The computed values are y(0.5)≈0.94818, y(1)≈1.29700 and y(2)≈1.47253. Its derivative is 3e−2t, which verifies y′+2y=3 exactly. Interpreting 3 as a steady input and 2y as proportional removal explains the shape: initially all input increases y, then removal catches up. The constant particular solution yp​=3/2 balances input and removal, and the homogeneous solution yh​=−23​e−2t is the transient response that corrects it to the initial condition. Because this autonomous differential equation has a time-independent right-hand side, 3/2 is also an equilibrium point.
The first panel adds the particular solution and homogeneous solution; the second shows the same balance in rates, 3=y′+2y. This links the algebra to a physical accounting rule. Newton's law of cooling has this form with a=k and b=kTa​, while an electrical circuit can have a varying input. In both cases the integrating factor systematically handles the input rather than requiring a guess for a particular solution.
Variable coefficients work just as directly. For y′+2ty=t, y(0)=0, the integrating factor is et2, and
(et2y)′=tet2,et2y(t)=21​(et2−1),y(t)=21​(1−e−t2).
(45)
Thus y(0.5)≈0.11060, y(1)≈0.31606 and y(2)≈0.49084. The derivative y′=te−t2 verifies y′+2ty=t, including at zero, where both coefficient and input vanish. No division by t is necessary. The general solution is y=1/2+Ce−t2: 1/2 is a constant particular solution, and Ce−t2 solves the associated homogeneous linear differential equation. Although this special forcing term admits a constant trajectory, this is a nonautonomous differential equation: it depends explicitly on time. Merely setting its right-hand side to zero at one instant would not establish a constant solution of a differential equation; at t=0 every state has zero slope.
The direction field shows the selected trajectory leaving its initially horizontal tangent line. For t≥0, the difference between any two solutions of a differential equation is multiplied by e−t2, rather than e−2t in the constant-rate example. This dependence on elapsed history is clearer if the exact formula is rewritten as
y(t)=y0​e−∫t0​t​a(u)du+∫t0​t​e−∫st​a(u)dub(s)ds.
(46)
For t≥t0​, each contribution from the input at s is weighted by the accumulated coefficient between s and t. The homogeneous solution remembers the initial condition; the particular solution given by the second term accumulates the forcing term with zero initial value. This decomposition differs from choosing a constant particular solution, but gives the same total. Initial-data memory tends to zero when ∫t0​t​a→+∞; a negative accumulated coefficient instead amplifies it. The reciprocal relation between integrating factor and homogeneous solution is developed in MIT's notes on solutions to linear first-order equations.
Why does the trick work? The fundamental theorem of calculus and chain rule give μ′=aμ. Consequently the product rule gives
(μy)′=μy′+μ′y=μ(y′+ay)=μb.
(47)
Integrating this identity and dividing by the positive exponential function μ produces the stated formula. Any nonzero constant multiple of μ works equally well; normalization is a convenience. This is the beauty of the method: a sum involving an unknown function becomes one exact derivative, leaving only an integral of known functions. See Oregon State's product-rule derivation. The related integrating factor for a differential one-form extends the idea of making an expression exact beyond this linear setting.

Limitations of integrating factors for second-order equations (w=exp∫(B−A′)/Adx)

Words: 73
Integrating factor OurBigBook.com
On an interval where A=0, the displayed factor gives
w(Ay′′+By′+Cy)=(wAy′)′+wCy.
(48)
This follows from (wA)′=wB. It gives a useful self-adjoint form but does not solve a general second-order ordinary differential equation, since the wCy term remains. If C=0, it does reduce to one integration for y′. Another reducible class has C=B′−A′′, because the original left side is then [Ay′+(B−A′)y]′. These are sufficient special cases, not a classification of all solvable equations.

Integrating factor OurBigBook.com
For y′+a(x)y=H(x) with continuous a, the integrating factor μ=exp(∫a) gives the displayed solution. It is continuous at the step and solves the differential equation classically on each side; the derivative jumps by one. The value assigned to the Heaviside step function at the single point zero does not affect the integral. A discontinuity in y would instead produce an unintended delta term in its distributional derivative.

Integrating factor for a differential one-form (∂x​(μf)=∂y​(μg))

Words: 223 Articles: 2
Integrating factor OurBigBook.com
For the differential one-form fdy+gdx, a nonzero integrating factor μ makes μfdy+μgdx an exact differential form locally. If it equals dF, then Fy​=μf, Fx​=μg, and equality of mixed partial derivatives gives the displayed compatibility condition. Conversely this condition is local sufficiency for smooth coefficients on a small rectangle; global exactness additionally depends on the domain. Zeros of the multiplying factor can change the solution set, so equivalence is asserted only where the factor is nonzero.

For a differential one-form Pdx+Qdy, seek a nonzero integrating factor μ(x). Expanding (μP)y​=(μQ)x​ gives the displayed equation where Q=0. Such a factor exists locally when (Py​−Qx​)/Q depends only on x, and is μ=exp∫[(Py​−Qx​)/Q]dx. Likewise, a factor depending only on y obeys μ′/μ=(Qx​−Py​)/P where P=0. The resulting product is an exact differential form on a sufficiently small regular domain; singular lines of the factor need separate treatment.

For a differential one-form Mdx+Ndy, a monomial integrating factor exists on a chosen domain away from the axes when constants α,β make
My​−Nx​=xα​N−yβ​M.

Three-state cyclic conversion model (A˙=−aA+cC,B˙=aA−bB,C˙=bB−cC)

Words: 165 Articles: 1
Linear system of differential equations OurBigBook.com
Three nonnegative amounts convert in the directed cycle A→B→C→A at positive first-order rates a,b,c. The linear system of ordinary differential equations conserves A+B+C=N. Its characteristic polynomial is λ[λ2+(a+b+c)λ+ab+bc+ca]. The two nonzero eigenvalues have negative real part, so every trajectory converges to the unique steady state with that total:
(A∞​,B∞​,C∞​)=ab+bc+caN​(bc,ca,ab).
(50)
This is also a column-convention continuous-time Markov chain after normalizing by N>0: every component loses to one successor and receives from one predecessor. A complex-conjugate pair produces damped oscillations about equilibrium even though the amounts remain nonnegative. A repeated nonzero eigenvalue is defective and requires a Jordan chain.

Defective repeated eigenvalue in a cyclic conversion model ((a+b+c)2=4(ab+bc+ca))

Words: 78
Three-state cyclic conversion model OurBigBook.com
When the displayed equality holds, the two nonzero eigenvalues of the three-state cyclic conversion model coincide at λ=−(a+b+c)/2. The positive cyclic rates force each eigenspace to have dimension at most one: if its A coordinate vanished, the first eigenvector equation would force C=0, and then the third would force B=0. Thus the repeated eigenvalue has only one eigenvector direction and the matrix is not diagonalizable. A length-two Jordan chain produces both eλt and teλt transients. The rates (a,b,c)=(1,4,1) give an explicit example with λ=−3.

Impulse cancellation of a harmonic oscillator

Words: 56
Jump condition for an impulse OurBigBook.com
For the harmonic oscillator equation y′′+ω2y=Jδ(t−t∗​), with ω>0, the displacement is continuous and the velocity increases by J at the impulse. If the incoming displacement is zero and J=−y′(t∗​−), the outgoing displacement and velocity both vanish. The subsequent homogeneous solution is identically zero. Equivalently, the causal forced response (J/ω)H(t−t∗​)sin(ω(t−t∗​)) cancels the pre-existing oscillation, where H is the Heaviside step function.
